body: I suspect the Windows code is failing to explicitly set the gRPC status code when it returns an error, so it's winding up UNKNOWN instead of UNAVAILABLE.  @nicolasnoble, can you please take a look?  Thanks!
@markdroth can you point me at the rough codepath that would do this properly on Unix?

I don't know offhand which codepath it is.  But given that the behavior changes based on Linux vs. Windows, it seems like it has to be some Windows-specific code that is not setting the error properly.  Maybe try reproducing the problem with the steps above and enabling a bunch of tracers to see where the status code is coming from on the Linux side?

I think what you're describing here is mostly working as intended. When a server socket is closed abruptly, the _underlying_ error messages received at the client may very well be platform-specific, gRPC doesn't make any guarantees about that. Those nested messages are generally for humans, not machines. Especially given that there's no reference for "platform A is correct, platform B is wrong, per [some spec]", it's not a bug that platforms differ in these implementation details.
I see. I didn't catch the top-level error code difference. I'll reopen this and chat with the team about what the right behavior is here, if there is a consistent story we should settle on.

issue.body:
Fixes #24206 by ensuring that IOCP/socket errors in the iomgr on_read callback are properly annotated with the gRPC Unavailable status. The WindowsEventEngine was already doing this correctly (try running the client with `$env:GRPC_EXPERIMENTS="event_engine_client"`).

This also adds two small cleanups:
 * Cleanly prints statuses with their child statuses in a few spots within the chttp2 transport logging (previously, child messages were printed with garbled bits)
 * Adds friendly names to a subset of WSA errors that we're likely to see from common operations. The top-level status message will no longer just say "WSA Error" in many cases.

CC @Hamza-Q

body: @Hamza-Q https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/33502 should fix the issue. Your reproduction case worked just fine, I confirmed by adding an `abort();` to the C++ greeter server and observing status codes in the C++ greeter client. Windows now shows error code 14 (`GRPC_STATUS_UNAVAILABLE`) with the message "Connection reset". I'm not equipped to test Python on Windows at the moment, but I suspect it'll work the same.
